newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Some oil cos scale back NYMEX crude trading.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Some oil cos scale back NYMEX crude trading.

text.p: Some big oil companies have cut back crude futures trading on New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) in recent months as an unusual arbitrage play has roiled the contract, according to oil market participants.

A pattern of hefty deliveries of unpopular foreign crude against the May and June contracts -- and expected to continue against the July contract -- has sown uncertainty in the marketplace, driving some major players to prune their paper positions in favor of more predictability in the physical market.

"We're cutting back on our paper positions, and there's a lot more outright (physical market) activity already," said one oil company trader who didn't want to named. "It's changing the way people do business."

Foreign crude deliveries against the May and June contracts were 2.73 million barrels and 2.349 million barrels, respectively, much of it Nigerian Bonny Light. Physical delivery against the contract typically is for small amounts and rarely of foreign crude grades, which is not economic to run for all refineries.

The expiry of the June contract on May 20 left Morgan Stanley Group Inc's oil trading arm stuck with the bulk of the foreign crude delivered. The July contract, which expires June 22, is likely to see at least one million barrels of the foreign crude re-delivered amid slack refiner demand for these grades, traders say.
"The foreign crude won't go away, it keeps re-circulating," a trader for a U.S. oil company says.

The snowball started rolling in late April, when relatively strong demand in the U.S. combined with lower costs of shipping crude from the Gulf Coast into the hub at Cushing, Okla., to encourage the deliveries or cheap foreign crude oil, traders said.

Since then, the same foreign barrels have been passed around between various U.S. traders like a hot potato, with only some finding buyers among refiners near to the Cushing, Texas, delivery point. As a consequence, crude storage tanks at Cushing are now replete with the unwanted crude, traders said.

"If the July/August spread stays in 'contango' at 20-30 cents, those barrels will stay in tankage because there's no incentive to take them out," a trader said. "Contango" is when forward delivery prices are higher than prompt-delivery prices, encouraging a build up in inventories for future sale.

Another consequence of the foreign crude delivery game is the rising price for exchange-for-physical (EFP) transactions. These are agreements to exchange a futures position for physical West Texas Intermediate and have been fetching unusually high premiums as traders rushed to escape paper positions to avoid the possibility of receiving a foreign crude instead of the benchmark West Texas Intermediate/Cushing.

Having been up at 25 cents or so over the past couple of months, the EFP premium has been running at around 13-15 cents in recent days, reflecting continued upward pressure on cash WTI, traders noted.
But for companies used to using the NYMEX as an efficent hedge against volatile prices, the EFP route is a costly way to avoid delivery of the unwanted foreign crude.
Some companies say privately that they are pushing the NYMEX to change its delivery mechanism to, effectively, make it uneconomic to deliver the foreign crude against the contract.
"People aren't happy with the differentials," a trader says. "Refiners are awfully finicky."

In the case of Bonny Light, for example, sellers received a premium of 60 cents a barrel upon delivery to account for the grade's quality difference with WTI. As part of a series of planned changes beginning with the July contract, that premium drops to 40 cents a barrel next month.
But that's still too high for some U.S. refiners which can't easily switch their diet from the West Texas Intermediate grade if they get stuck with foreign barrels.
A NYMEX spokesperson says the exchange continues to watch the market to ensure that the differentials are accurate.

"We have a delivery mechanism that's designed to be credible and consistent with the cash market," the spokesperson says. "We constantly monitor the market to make sure that the differentials are an accurate reflection of the cash market over a period of time."
The spokesperson gave no indication, however, of any impending changes related to the foreign deliveries.
--New York Energy Desk ((+1 212 859 1620))
